items.before:
Stepwells gave communities in dry western India year-round access to water, and became places to gather, rest and worship. Rani-ki-Vav, on the banks of the Saraswati river in Patan, is one of the finest.

It was built in the 11th century during the rule of the Chaulukya (Solanki) dynasty, and is traditionally linked to Queen Udayamati. Its stepped corridors and pavilions carry hundreds of sculptures, many of them of Vishnu and his avatars. Silt from the river buried it for centuries, which helped preserve the carving.
items.after:
Stepwells gave communities in drier areas year-round access to water. They also became places to gather, rest, and even worship. Rani-ki-Vav, in the Patan area, is one of India's finest.

It was built in the 11th century during the rule of the Chaulukya (Solanki) dynasty. It is traditionally linked to Queen Udayamati.

Its stepped corridors and pavilions carry hundreds of sculptures – many of them of Vishnu Bhagwan and his avatars. Silt from the river buried it for centuries, which helped preserve the carvings.

items.before:
Havelis are traditional townhouses and mansions found across western and northern India, especially in Gujarat and Rajasthan. Many are built around inner courtyards that keep the house cool and private.

Their street facades are often richly carved, with overhanging balconies and enclosed windows (jharokhas) from which the family could watch the life of the street.
items.after:
Havelis are traditional townhouses or mansions found across India – especially in Gujarat and Rajasthan.

Many are built around inner courtyards that keep the house cool and private.

Their street facades are often richly carved with overhanging balconies and enclosed windows from which the family could watch the life of the street.

items.before:
Dholavira is one of the largest known cities of the Harappan (Indus–Sarasvati) civilisation, on an island in the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat.

Its builders laid out a fortified citadel and a town, and managed scarce water with an elaborate system of channels and reservoirs. A large inscription in the Harappan script was found near one of its gateways.
items.after:
Dholavira is one of the largest known cities of the Harappan (Indus-Sarasvati) civilization. It is in the Kutch area of Gujarat.

Its builders laid out a fortified citadel and town. They managed scarce water through an elaborate system of channels and reservoirs.

items.before: For seven hundred years, monks and artisans carved prayer halls and monasteries straight into the living rock of a river gorge — then the jungle hid them for more than a thousand more.
items.after: For seven hundred years, monks and artisans carved prayer halls and monasteries directly into a gorge – then the jungle hid them for more than a thousand years.

items.before:
Around thirty caves line a horseshoe bend of the Waghur river. The earliest were carved around the 2nd century BCE; a second great wave of work followed in the 5th century CE. Some are viharas, monasteries where monks lived and studied. Others are chaityas, prayer halls built around a stupa.

Their wall paintings — courtly scenes, animals, stories of the Buddha's past lives — are among the most important surviving examples of ancient Indian painting. Abandoned and overgrown, the caves were brought to wider attention in 1819.
items.after:
Around thirty caves line a bend of the Waghur River in Maharashtra.

The earliest halls were carved around the 2nd century BCE. Some became monasteries where monks lived and studied while others became prayer halls for the public.

The wall paintings of courtly scenes, animals, and stories of avatars are amongst the most important surviving examples of ancient Indian painting.
